Every licensee of a long-term care home shall ensure that residents with a change of 5 per cent of body weight, or more, over one month; a change of 7.5 per cent of body weight, or more, over three months; a change of 10 per cent of body weight, or more, over six months; and any other weight change that compromises the resident's health status are assessed using an interdisciplinary approach, and that actions are taken and outcomes are evaluated. per_question.answer: The infection prevention and control lead is designated by the licensee to manage and oversee the infection prevention and control program. This role includes managing the program's development and implementation, overseeing education delivery to staff, caregivers, volunteers, visitors, and residents, conducting audits of infection prevention and control practices, conducting infectious disease surveillance, convening the Outbreak Management Team and interdisciplinary infection prevention and control team, reviewing information and screening results, and implementing required improvements to the program. The lead must have education and experience in various areas including infectious diseases, cleaning and disinfection, data collection and trend analysis, reporting protocols, outbreak management, asepsis, microbiology, adult education, epidemiology, and program management. [2]
cited: O. Reg. 246/22, s. 102 (Infection prevention and control program)

per_question.answer: The continence care and bowel management program must provide treatments and interventions to promote continence, treatments and interventions to prevent constipation including nutrition and hydration protocols, toileting programs with protocols for bowel management, strategies to maximize residents' independence, comfort, and dignity, including equipment, supplies, devices, and assistive aids. Additionally, it must ensure each resident who is incontinent receives an assessment that includes identification of causal factors, patterns, type of incontinence, and potential to restore function with specific interventions. Each resident who is incontinent must have an individualized plan in their plan of care to promote and manage bowel and bladder continence based on the assessment. Each resident who is unable to toilet independently some or all of the time must receive assistance from staff to manage and maintain continence. Residents who are incontinent and have been assessed as potentially continent or continent some of the time must receive assistance and support from staff to become continent or continent some of the time. Continence care products are not used as an alternative to providing assistance to a person to toilet. A range of continence care products must be available and accessible to residents and staff at all times, in sufficient quantities for all required changes. Residents who require continence care products must have sufficient changes to remain clean, dry, and comfortable. Residents are provided with a range of continence care products that are based on their individual assessed needs, properly fit the residents, promote resident comfort, ease of use, dignity, and good skin integrity, promote continued independence wherever possible, and are appropriate for the time of day and for the individual resident's type of incontinence. [1] [2] [3]
cited: O. Reg. 246/22, s. 56 (Continence care and bowel management)

per_question.answer: A person who has reasonable grounds to suspect that any of the following has occurred or may occur shall immediately report the suspicion and the information upon which it is based to the Director: 1. per_question.answer: A resident can be restrained by a physical device as described in paragraph 3 of subsection 34 (1) of the Fixing Long-Term Care Act, 2021, if the restraining of the resident is included in the resident's plan of care. cited: Fixing Long-Term Care Act, 2021, s. 35 (Restraining by physical devices)

per_question.answer: People at risk of pressure injuries should be repositioned every 2-4 hours [1]. This recommendation is based on evidence from randomized controlled trials and naturalistic studies, indicating that repositioning reduces the duration of pressure on tissues and decreases the risk of pressure injuries [1]. Additionally, the support surface and person or caregiver perspective should be considered when planning repositioning, ensuring that the frequency aligns with the person's goals and comfort [2]. Existing pressure injuries should also be considered when planning repositioning, as they may require different repositioning strategies [2].
cited: Pressure Injury Management: Risk Assessment, Prevention and Treatment (4th ed.), PDF p. 49 (Recommendations)

per_question.answer: The boxed warning for metformin states that it is associated with lactic acidosis, which can lead to death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. Symptoms include malaise, myalgias, respiratory distress, somnolence, and abdominal pain. Laboratory abnormalities include elevated blood lactate levels, anion gap acidosis, increased lactate/pyruvate ratio; and metformin plasma levels generally >5 mcg/mL. [1]
cited: Drug label: metformin er 500 mg > Boxed Warning
